name: batch-integration
context: Two enterprise systems have to stay in sync — an ERP and a CRM, a SaaS platform and a mainframe, a supplier portal and a data warehouse — and the movement of records between them is bulk rather than conversational. A nightly load, a periodic full extract plus delta, a partner's SFTP drop, a nightly Bulk API submission. Synchronous point-to-point integration is the wrong shape here: it would mean one HTTP round trip per record, it would require the source to be available whenever the consumer runs, and it would make a partner's rate limit the throughput ceiling. Batch integration instead treats data movement as a scheduled reconciliation of two systems of record over a defined window: gather a cohort of records, transform them, load them, then reconcile. Microsoft's cross-industry data integration guidance frames it exactly as this — 'scheduled or manual trigger, great for messaging services and asynchronous patterns, fewer individual packages and less message traffic', trading 'data freshness is lower' and a burst of load on the receiving system for scalability. The mechanics are more specific than 'run a job': a batch scope splits an inbound payload into records and writes them to a persistent queue (Mule's Batch Job Load-and-Dispatch phase), runs one or more steps that pull blocks of records in parallel, and a final report phase counts successes and failures (Mule's On Complete). Records that fail a step are not lost — Mule's acceptPolicy routes ONLY_FAILURES to a later step, and maxFailedRecords halts the job so a poison cohort is quarantined rather than retried forever. Where the batch must be large, Mule's Block Size determines how many records are pulled and processed as a unit, and Bulk API 2.0-style bulk endpoints on the target let a whole batch land in one asynchronous job instead of N inserts.
benefits: Record count stops being the throughput constraint: one bulk or file operation moves thousands of records where point-to-point would need thousands of round trips
The source and target only need to be simultaneously available during the batch window, so neither system must be kept up for the other
Bulk endpoints and file drops hit the target's efficient path rather than its interactive one, protecting the target's user-facing latency during the load
Delta-plus-snapshot semantics make the integration idempotent and recoverable: a consumer that falls behind can skip deltas and apply the latest snapshot to reset itself
Per-record error isolation with failure policies lets a small number of bad records be quarantined and reprocessed instead of aborting a whole window
A persistent record queue makes the job resumable — if the application is redeployed or crashes mid-run, execution resumes at the point it stopped rather than starting over
Batch windows are a natural place to put control totals, checksums, reject files, and reconciliation, which point-to-point flows tend to skip
Watermarks make replay safe: persist the successful watermark only after the batch completes, so a partial failure re-reads rather than skips
tradeoffs: Data is stale by design — a change made after the window closes is invisible to the target until the next run, and downstream users must be told the freshness bound

The receiving system takes a load spike inside the window, and Salesforce's own guidance is to insulate source and target during batch processing because contention can fail a user's update or a partial batch load
Recovering from a mid-window failure is an operational discipline, not a library call: the watermark must be withheld until completion or the next run silently skips the unprocessed tail
Bulk endpoints are asynchronous with their own job lifecycle, so the integration must poll or subscribe for job completion rather than assume a synchronous result
Batch scopes restructure an integration flow into phases with their own semantics, and records plus attributes created inside the scope do not propagate to downstream processors outside it

Large record counts demand explicit memory decisions — streaming an aggregator handles millions of records, but a fixed-size aggregator holds arrays in memory and disables random access when streaming
Partial-success semantics leak into the contract: consumers must handle 'this record failed and this one succeeded' rather than a simple success or failure
Batch is the wrong answer when the business need is a genuine real-time reaction, and forcing it there produces an architecture nobody can reason about
use_cases: Nightly change-data-capture extract from an ERP into a CRM using source-timestamp watermarks with a deliberate overlap window
Full snapshot of a SaaS product catalog into a data warehouse, where a snapshot lets the consumer skip missed deltas and reset
Partner SFTP file drop parsed into records, registered with batch metadata, parked for a throttle window, then dispatched to processing
Bulk API 2.0 submission of 50,000 account updates with an asynchronous job that must be polled to completion
Rejected-record reprocessing: a resubmission flow that reads only records in READY state from an error table and re-runs them
Reconciling a SaaS platform against an on-premises mainframe inside a maintenance window, with control totals checked on arrival
avoid_when: A user or downstream system needs to see a change immediately — batching exists to trade freshness for throughput, so this inverts the purpose
Neither side can guarantee a stable window, and the target has no capacity headroom for the burst the batch will create
The volume is small enough that a scheduled job costs more operational attention than a few point-to-point calls
You cannot implement idempotent replay — without idempotency, a re-run after partial failure duplicates records in the target
The integration is conversational (request, response, user waiting) rather than reconciliatory
There is no owner for the failure path — batch windows accumulate silent failures unless someone reconciles and reprocesses rejects
component_types: Batch Job Scope: the container that splits an inbound payload into records, persists them, executes steps, and emits a completion report
Record Queue / Stepping Queue: the persistent store holding records between phases so a crashed run resumes rather than restarts
Batch Step: a processing phase that pulls blocks of records in parallel and applies one transformation or system call
Batch Aggregator: the optional terminal component that collects records into fixed-size arrays or a stream for a single bulk call
Record Filter / Accept Policy: the routing rule that sends records failing a prior step (ONLY_FAILURES) to a later step instead of dropping them
maxFailedRecords / Quarantine: the guard that halts a job once the failure count crosses a threshold, and the reject store the failures land in
Watermark / Control Total: the persisted position marker and reconciliation metadata that make a partial window safely replayable
Parking Lot / Throttle Table: the staging table that holds registered batches and controls how many are processed concurrently
Scheduler / Trigger: the cron, file-arrival, or event trigger that opens the batch window
technology_stack: Mule Batch Job / Batch Step / Batch Aggregator
anti_patterns: Watermark advanced before the batch completes, so a partial failure causes the next window to skip unprocessed records silently
Loading during business hours with no capacity headroom, so the batch contends with interactive traffic and fails users' updates
A single monolithic batch step that transforms, calls the target, and reports together, leaving no seam to reprocess only the failures
Fixed-size aggregator on a very large record set, exhausting memory where streaming would not
No maxFailedRecords bound — a poison record causes the window to retry forever and the job never converges
Assuming a bulk endpoint returns synchronously, so the integration records success before the target's asynchronous job has actually finished
Treating the batch as the default: applied to low-volume conversational integration, it adds windows, watermarks, and failure paths for no throughput gain
Aggregating records across batch steps and expecting the modification to be visible to the next step — it is not
design_principles: Windows, not streams, when reconciliation is the goal: a batch window is an explicit, bounded agreement about when data will be consistent
Idempotent replay is a precondition, not a nice-to-have — every step must tolerate being run twice over the same cohort
Quarantine, do not retry forever: bound the failure count and route rejects somewhere a human or a later run can see them
Withhold the watermark until completion, so a crashed window re-reads rather than skips
Separate snapshot from delta: a delta is cheap and incremental, a snapshot is the escape hatch that lets a lagging consumer reset without replaying everything
Separate data from metadata: keep file identity, producer, tenant, sequence number, and type in a metadata store so the consumer can order and validate without parsing payloads
Bulk endpoints for bulk loads: use the target's asynchronous bulk mechanism rather than looping its interactive API
Declare the freshness bound: consumers must know how stale the data can be, and that number is a contract
best_practices: Use source-timestamp watermarks with a deliberate overlap window, because source timestamps can be delayed and commits can race the schedule
Persist or externally record the successful watermark only after the batch has completed
Use change data capture against source tables rather than full extracts where the target tolerates incremental updates
Name, checksum, control-total, archive, and reject-file handling for every file-based hop
Chunk or stream large files instead of loading a very large payload into a single in-memory transformation
Poll or subscribe for asynchronous bulk job completion, and treat 'submitted' as distinct from 'applied'
Monitor per-window success counts, failure counts, and reject counts, and alert when a window's failure ratio moves
Schedule batch windows against measured target capacity, and prefer off-peak windows where the target has no headroom
